overview: The Fatimids were an Ismaili Shi‘i dynasty whose caliphate began in North Africa in 909 and moved its centre to Egypt after conquering it in 969. Cairo became their capital in 973. Their political rule ended in 1171: the imported map’s continuation to 1279 must not be read as continued Fatimid government.

periods.title: North African beginnings
periods.summary: The dynasty ruled from North African capitals before its conquest of Egypt.

periods.title: Egypt and Cairo
periods.summary: Cairo became the dynastic capital; Fustat remained an important centre of production.

items.text: Cairo’s al-Azhar mosque was built in 969 to 973. Later Fatimid projects included al-Aqmar mosque, built in 1125, and the monumental gates associated with the vizier Badr al-Jamali. These are successive building campaigns, not one construction project.

Fustat’s makers produced ceramics, glass, metalwork and carved wood. Egyptian potters refined lustre decoration already developed in Iraq: its shimmering surface shows skilled adaptation, rather than proof that Egypt invented the technique.

A bowl painted with an eagle, made in Egypt around 1000, survives in the Met as 63.178.1. Metallic lustre was applied over its white glazed earthenware. The bird spreads across a useful household form that could also display remarkable craftsmanship.

A tiny writing sample appears on that bowl: مسلم, “Muslim,” the potter’s name. The Arabic signature occurs below the eagle and on the base. Similar signatures appear on many vessels; they may identify a maker or a workshop, rather than every piece being one person’s work.

A carved rock-crystal piece attributed to Egypt in the ninth or tenth century may once have held perfume. Its date overlaps the period before Fatimid rule. The Met explains how Egyptian crystal objects later travelled into European church treasuries, sometimes acquiring new uses as reliquaries.

An eleventh-century Egyptian gold earring, only about 3.5 centimetres high, combines fine wires with tiny granules. Its loops once supported further ornaments. Looking closely reveals the labour hidden in jewellery that can fit in a hand.

The Cairo Genizah preserved discarded writings from the Ben Ezra synagogue in Fustat. Among the surviving fragments are prescriptions, medical books and drug lists. This unusual archive lets us see individual worries and practical tasks that royal monuments rarely record.

Prescription Or.1081 J39, dated to the eleventh or twelfth century, combines Arabic writing with Judaeo-Arabic: Arabic language written in Hebrew letters. Numerals in Hebrew letters record quantities. A pharmacist needed to understand a working document, not merely admire beautiful handwriting.

That prescription called for ingredients to be ground and mixed with rose syrup, and mentioned a chicken diet. It records historical medical practice, not a remedy to try today. The editors suggest a possible identity for its patient, but cannot securely establish it.

A traveller in Alexandria wrote to a cousin in the Maghreb about illness, danger and longing to return home. The Judaeo-Arabic draft, Bodleian MS heb. b 11/7, makes long-distance travel feel less like a line on a map and more like missing your family.

The traveller used the back of a Fatimid fiscal document dated 1106 to 1107. Reusing paper preserved two different stories together: government accounting on one side, private anxiety on the other. That earlier account also helps date the letter.

Around 1019, Mevorakh ibn Yazdad was appointed to oversee guardians managing a merchant’s minor child’s inheritance. Later disputes involved both Jewish and Muslim courts. This is concrete evidence that a child’s property could require adults, documents and prolonged legal argument.

ending.text: Saladin ended the Fatimid caliphate in 1171 after the death of al-Adid. Ayyubid rule followed in Egypt. Cairo, its inhabitants and its craft traditions continued; a change of dynasty did not erase the city or the communities whose documents survive.
